Faculty of Electric Power Engineering, Kunming University of Science and Technology, Kunming 650500, China) Abstract: With the rapid growth of installed photovoltaic (PV) generation capacity, the influence of harmonics in PV power stations on power system stability has become more and more prominent, making harmonic mitigation a key issue for ensuring secure grid operation. This paper systematically summarizes the harmonic generation mechanisms, classification methods, modeling techniques, analysis approaches, and mitigation strategies for PV power stations. In the mechanism analysis, attention is paid not only to the dominant role of grid-connected inverters, but also to the multi-source coupling characteristics involving auxiliary equipment within the station and background harmonic excitations. On modeling methods, the advantages, disadvantages, and applicable scenarios of mechanism-based modeling, data-driven modeling, and hybrid modeling are compared, highlighting the application potential of hybrid modeling under complex working conditions. In terms of harmonic analysis, measurement-based and simulation-based approaches are distinguished, and suitable combinations of analysis methods are proposed for different scale PV power stations. Harmonic mitigation technologies are discussed from three aspects: active filtering, passive filtering, and hybrid filtering, and their respective mechanisms and engineering applicability are expounded. Finally, future trends are discussed, including the development of intelligent harmonic analysis and the transition of harmonic mitigation toward source suppression and coordinated governance. Recommendations such as lifecycle management and improvement of standards are also proposed. This work is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 62263014). Key words: photovoltaic power station; harmonics; harmonic analysis; harmonic mitigation

Xi\u2019an Key Laboratory of Electrical Equipment Condition Monitoring and Power Supply Safety, Xi\u2019an 710054, China) Abstract: To address the challenges posed by the increasing scale and structural complexity of modern distribution networks, and to effectively evaluate node criticality for enhancing system operational reliability, this paper proposes an intra-regional node criticality assessment method that comprehensively considers both electrical characteristics and topological structure. First, based on the node impedance matrix and sensitivity matrix, a criticality index reflecting the electrical characteristics of nodes is proposed. By combining local and global topological structures, a topological criticality index is proposed to characterize the structural importance of nodes. These indices are combined to construct an electro-topological coupling matrix (ETCM). Then, based on the ETCM, a comprehensive node criticality index incorporating both electrical and topological properties is proposed to evaluate node criticality using system-wide information. A two-level partitioning strategy combining the threshold method and Gaussian kernel function is developed to divide the distribution network into multiple subregions. Finally, the criticality of nodes within each subregion is assessed using the corresponding sub electro-topological coupling matrix (SETCM), enabling a more reasonable evaluation of node importance from a regional perspective. Simulations on the modified IEEE 33-node system demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in assessing node criticality. This work is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 52577138). Key words: distribution network; electrical-characteristic criticality index; topological-structure criticality index; electro-topological coupling matrix; partitioning strategy; node criticality assessment

The twin concept first found practical application in NASA's Apollo space program where spacecraft simulations were run on Earth-based replicas to predict and manage space program [11]. Subsequently, Dr. Grieves further developed the concept of DT [12]. Initially, DT application focused primarily on process systems, spanning from production to forecasting and post-management [13]. The capabilities of DT in modeling, prediction, simulation, and optimal operation offer a promising solution for ADNs requiring unconventional operations. Beyond more monitoring, DT supports DER generation, load forecasting, and proactive consideration of potential operational issues within the distribution network. In a virtual environment, DT systems collect real-time data from physical networks and, together with pre-existing data, suggest the most appropriate solutions for real-world applications. By leveraging real-world data, DT can improve the accuracy and reliability of these algorithms. The CST supports the integration of a substantial pipeline of proposed projects, including 46 GW of wind, 33 GW of solar, and 10 GW of hydro, effectively doubling the existing capacity [190]. By providing a detailed source of energy data and modeling, the connection simulation tool integrates the power system to accelerate the development process and manage potential risks before proceeding with the grid connection process.General Electric (GE) is a leading company in the digitization of manufacturing leveraging the IoT to analyze and collect vast amounts of data from machines, and its DT platform is illustrated in Fig. 8. GE gathers and analyzes data from sensors embedded in its manufactured and sold equipment, implementing this data as a DT to enable virtual monitoring and control services. GE has developed Predix, a big data platform intended for applications across multiple industries, although the number of applications in power generation remains smaller compared to other sectors. GE's DT technology for power generation offers advanced predictive maintenance and optimal management support, including power plant lifetime management, anomaly detection, improvement of generation efficiency (such as thermal efficiency), and response to one-time events. The company has also introduced the concept of \u201Cdigital substation\u201D which extends the maintenance optimization function of existing asset performance management software to the broader power grid. While GE's maintenance platform for individual power plants and core facilities demonstrates leading technology based on smart factory applications, limitations exist in applying these solutions on a macro level, such as grid-level emulation. First, the current application of DT in power systems is primarily focused on monitoring systems. A DT environment capable of replicating real system performance can enable not only simple simulation but also more advanced evaluation of actual system behaviors. For instance, implementing AC/DC hybrid networks remains challenging due to the need for high-end equipment, which poses financial and technical limitations. Hence, continual verification through DT environments is essential to bridge this gap. As DC facilities increase, different failure analyses will be needed, with the DT environment offering more accurate verification than traditional simulation-based assessments. Additionally, a DT can facilitate preemptive evaluations, such as distribution system capacity analysis and system impact assessment, particularly as DERs increase. The results of these studies confirm that wind-GESS integration is technically, economically, and environmentally viable in a variety of energy systems.A typical industrial customer consumes significant electricity daily, and appliances and equipment require large amounts of power. Increasing customer demand fees allow for the continuation of peak demand. Industrial consumers usually consume their maximum energy and demand over 15 min, so their charges are based on their maximum demand [262]. The peak demand charges allow the budget bill to be covered by half. As with energy arbitrage, peak shaving is somewhat similar; however, the difference is that it does not have an economic purpose, whereas energy arbitrage does. A peak shaving system uses ESS to support peak demand. The customer side installs peak shaving applications, while the supplier installs energy arbitrage applications. During peak power periods, the grid is under more significant stress, which reduces its overall efficiency. In microgrids, operators sometimes use diesel generators to achieve peak shaving of 10 % [263]. When peak demand is met, the cost of operating and maintaining microgrids increases because of the additional fuel consumption and CO2 emissions [262]. Therefore, peak shaving is of great importance in the current era of research.Energy Storage Systems (ESS) can provide these voltage support systems most effectively. Real-time voltage stabilization can be achieved using ESS by rapidly injecting or absorbing reactive power. In the power system, ESS maximizes efficiency by reducing transmission losses and providing localized voltage support to minimize the need for reactive power transfer over long distances [270]. Since renewable energy sources such as solar and wind are intermittent, voltage fluctuations can be more common in regions with low voltage stability, making ESS a valuable addition in grids with high levels of renewable energy integration [272]. Voltage regulation is crucial for grid stability, and ESS can deliver an effective and reliable solution to keep voltage within desired limits. As a component of modern voltage management strategies, ESS provides immediate reactive power support, ensuring the stable operation of the power system.ESS's ability to respond rapidly and provide consistent power makes it an ideal resource for applications involving black starts. ESS has become increasingly crucial in black start scenarios as power systems incorporate renewable energy sources that may be less predictable [276]. As a result of ESS, the power grid is more resilient and reliable, facilitating faster recovery from blackouts. During blackouts, black start capabilities are crucial for minimizing the impact and restoring power as quickly as possible. ESS makes recovery more efficient by providing crucial voltage support, maintaining balance, and assisting conventional generators in starting [277]. As a result, ESS is an effective tool for ensuring a reliable and resilient power system.A coordinated voltage compensation approach using multiple distributed ESS units has been proposed to enhance grid stability in RE-rich grids. This method assigns voltage compensation responsibilities to each distributed ESS unit in each grid region according to strategic segmentation. Synchronizing and coordinating control across these ESS units prevents overregulation and allows the units to compensate for voltage fluctuations as needed, providing support when needed to other units [297]. In grids with concentrated RE penetration, ESS voltage compensation was optimized using localized SOC control methods. This system maintains a stable voltage across all network nodes by controlling each ESS's power output based on its SOC [298]. A modern, coordinated strategy for voltage regulation with distributed ESS maintains grid stability while increasing renewable integration with an adaptive, reliable solution.An electric microgrid is a self-sustaining electrical network with a well-defined geographical footprint, frequently implemented in neighborhoods, schools, and office buildings. The energy storage system (ESS) and loads are also part of the network. The network comprises power generation sources, distribution infrastructure, and ESS. Microgrids can achieve self-sufficiency, energy arbitrage, and carbon reduction benefits with an integrated energy management system. There are two modes of operation for microgrids grid-connected (where they exchange power with main grids) and isolated (where they operate independently). ESS must support these functions and increase microgrid reliability and flexibility. Both studies [309,310] investigated the integration of wind and PV solar power sources into an AC microgrid. A combination of AC power supplies and renewable sources such as wind and PV allows for the effective integration of renewable energy sources, stabilizing the power supply and managing variable generation patterns. With this setup, the ESS quickly absorbs excess energy or provides stored energy when wind or solar production fluctuates, maintaining a steady power supply.Reference [311] proposes a DC microgrid with dual ESSs, including a battery pack and a supercapacitor, to provide DC loads when a solar grid powers a PV solar system. This configuration, which is optimized for PV generation, simplifies the system structure and enhances power efficiency. ESSs can also stabilize a DC microgrid by providing rapid discharging capabilities through supercapacitors and sustained RE through batteries for wind power integration in a DC microgrid. Studies [312,313] also introduced a DC microgrid modified to handle AC and DC loads by integrating an AC/DC inverter. This inverter converts DC power generated by solar and wind sources into AC power for AC loads. This versatile configuration allows wind power to be utilized successfully, especially when coupled with an ESS, which compensates for wind speed changes, smooths out energy output, and ensures a continuous power supply. By integrating ESS into these AC/DC microgrid setups, wind and PV solar energy can be captured to their fullest potential. Combined with batteries and supercapacitors, the storage technologies respond rapidly to voltage fluctuations and support reliable energy distribution across AC andDC systems.Wind power fluctuations are difficult to control because of their intermittent and unpredictable nature. Depending on the magnitude of the fluctuations, voltage instability, frequency deviations, and operational inefficiencies could impact the quality and reliability of electricity supplied to consumers. With this in mind, ESS has emerged as an essential tool for smoothing out electricity fluctuations. They provide flexible support to absorb excess power during peak periods and release it during low wind periods [325]. Advanced control algorithms can be incorporated into ESS to improve operator efficiency and reliability by regulating wind power output while ensuring consistent energy delivery. Many algorithms offer unique advantages in mitigating wind power fluctuations, including filtering, moving averages, discrete Fourier Transforms (DFT), Kalman filters, empirical mode decompositions (EMD), wavelet decompositions, and model MPC [326\u2013329]. Based on real-time responsiveness, accurate prediction, and multi-scale analysis, each algorithm provides ESS with specific benefits that allow it to tailor its performance to grid and wind power profile-specific needs. By integrating these algorithms strategically, ESS can improve the efficiency of managing power fluctuations and support the integration of renewable energy sources into modern power systems.A circular economy is also supported by policy and research on sustainable recycling and end-of-life management of ESS components. A critical emerging area of cybersecurity is digitally connected ESS networks, ensuring protection from cyber threats. Furthermore, AI-based forecasting models are integrated into ESS control systems to improve renewable generation and load predictions. Funding Texts: Funding text 1: This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea ( NRF ) grant funded by the Korea government ( MSIT ) (No. RS-2022-NR070842 ), and also supported by the Basic Research Project ( GP2025-005 ) of the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources ( KIGAM ).; Funding text 2: South Korea is located in a temperate monsoon climate zone, where securing sufficient summer precipitation is essential to ensure water availability during the subsequent dry season (Chang and Chung, 2021; Rahman et al., 2025). The overall characteristics of the East Asian monsoon over the Korean Peninsula are projected to change, including intensified and seasonally shifted precipitation, increased evapotranspiration, and more frequent extreme events (Kim et al., 2023; Seo et al., 2013). These shifts may ultimately reduce groundwater recharge and the overall amount of available groundwater, while increasing its temporal variability (Meixner et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2020). To support groundwater resource management under changing climate conditions, the Korea Water Resources Corporation (K-Water) operates the National Groundwater Monitoring Network (NGMN). At the point scale, the ability of AI models to capture nonlinear relationships between GWL and changing climate conditions has led to their widespread application at national monitoring wells (Haider et al., 2023; Jeong and Park, 2019; Kim et al., 2021; Yoon et al., 2013). However, to the best of the authors\u2019 knowledge, no study has yet applied AI-based approaches to simulate long-term GWL changes at monitoring wells from the NGMN under climate change scenarios, and how different aquifer types respond to these conditions remains poorly understood.By applying SHAP to the final 1D-CNN model, we were able to identify the relationships between input variables and outputs that were learned by the model. However, SHAP values represent the statistical contribution to model predictions and do not directly explain causal relationships (Ma and Tourani, 2020). For example, while higher temperature and lower relative humidity values resulted in negative SHAP values, indicating a negative influence on the GWL, this result alone does not imply that rising temperature or decreasing relative humidity are the direct causes of GWL decline. In this study, only climatic inputs were used and other factors that could influence GWL variations such as stream interactions and regional groundwater flow were not considered. Therefore, caution is required when interpreting SHAP values as indicators of actual GWL drivers. In some wells, a limited number of high rainfall events were linked to negative SHAP values, indicating that not all rainfall events contributed to GWL. This may reflect infiltration limitation due to soil saturation or surface runoff during heavy rainfall events, thus preventing infiltration and groundwater recharge (Tashie et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2019). Despite some exceptions, the overall SHAP value patterns were consistent with hydrogeological processes. Specifically, the pattern in which higher temperatures and lower relative humidity values negatively influence GWL reflects a process where increased evapotranspiration leads to reduced groundwater recharge or direct groundwater evaporation, ultimately resulting in GWL decline. In contrast, higher rainfall values, acting as a climatic driver that promotes groundwater recharge, were associated with positive SHAP values and correspondingly higher GWL. While direct causality cannot be established, the observed SHAP patterns suggest that the model captures hydrogeologically plausible processes, supporting the reliability of future GWL projections.This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Korea government (MSIT) (No.RS-2022-NR070842), and also supported by the Basic Research Project (GP2025-005) of the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources (KIGAM).

Funding Texts: Funding text 1: Based on the analysis of previously published review papers, it has been observed that the majority do not comprehensively address recent advancements in V2X technology and its integrations, particularly those involving AI. To address this identified gap, this review paper provides an overview of the latest advancements in all V2X integrations (V2G, V2B, V2L, V2V), applicable AI strategies, human intention, electricity market, as well as the maritime transportation sector (Vehicle-to-Ship (V2S)). Furthermore, the challenges and future research directions for each integration are examined and analyzed. In addition, official standards, published datasets, and recently funded projects supported by organizations such as U.S. Department of Energy (DoE), U.S. Department of Transportation (DoT), Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC), and European Union Commission (EUC) are presented and discussed. The overall contributions of this review paper are outlined as follows: ; Funding text 2: This work is supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC), Discovery Grant stream (with the grant identification number RGPIN-2020-05513), and the University of Windsor, Canada. ; Funding text 3: China\u2019s Grid-Connected EV Pilot Projects, funded by the National Development and Reform Commission, aim to stabilize the power grid by using EVs as batteries, implementing 30 V2G pilots in nine cities and integrating EVs into power trading systems. Singapore\u2019s Developing Critical Intelligent Modules for Large-scale V2G Implementation, backed by EMA and the Singapore Institute of Technology with $20 million, tests V2G technology using 15 commercial vans and 10 V2G-enabled chargers to assess grid services and regulatory feasibility. Another Singapore-based project, the SP Group V2G Trial, evaluates V2G integration at four charging points to enhance grid reliability. In Thailand, the Nissan V2G Project at Chulalongkorn University, supported by multiple partners, studies sustainable energy management through Nissan LEAF\u2019s bi-directional charging, analyzing energy flow and cost-saving potential. ; Funding text 4: The authors would like to express their deepest gratitude to the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) for supporting this work through Discovery Grant Stream with the grant identification number RGPIN-2020-05513. Funding Texts: Unfortunately, today, wind and PV generators only partially meet the previous Brundtland and IEA definitions due to the processes and materials used for the construction of the generation systems (e.g. PV panels, wind turbine blades), the generator installation (e.g. PV panel supports, foundations for the turbines), the maintenance, the decommissioning and so on, that prevent a fully sustainable energy production [7,8]. Moreover, the land transformation due to their installation also negatively affects their sustainability [9]. To face their variable and intermittent power generation and to properly integrate them into the electrical network as well as to exploit their benefits (e.g. they could be installed next to the loads) the Transmission System Operators (TSOs) and Distribution System Operators (DSOs) are introducing new matters whose impact on sustainability must be cared. In detail, it is necessary to account for the impact on sustainability due to the introduction of energy storage systems (ESSs) [10], automation systems and sensor networks [11], digital infrastructures [12], and so on, as well as the upgrade of the electrical network infrastructures, distribution networks management systems and so on [7,13]. Finally, it is worth noting that global electricity demand is increasing faster than renewable power generation [14], thus, a substantial change of course is necessary. Additionally, to obtain an effective SEE is also necessary to limit the energy losses along the overall power system chain and to make each ring and involved process sustainable [ 15\u201317].The concurrent adoption of MFOM and PFOM can help the AI to understand how to move towards a full SEE. It is worth noticing that this approach embraces technology neutrality and enables accounting for technology advancements toward better sustainability (e.g. passing from fossil to green diesel [52]). Moreover, an advantage of this approach is the holistic view of sustainability that combines the life cycle assessment (LCA) [53,54] and exploitable electrical energy. Fig. 2 reports a typical LCA flow that comprises its key aspects and steps [55]. Although in the following, MFOM and PFOM will be used to support the analysis of AI contribution in SEE, other LCA indexes could be adopted. The use of other indexes can not change the validity and the conclusions of the following discussion. In fact, whatever the index, it must evaluate positively each AI contribution toward an increased exploitable electrical energy and improved sustainability, as the considered ones do.In such a context, AI is very useful at the power system planning stage because it can support a geographic estimation of power demand growth of the different loads (ac and dc), as well as forecasting the RPG production also cross-checking data about planned and potential new generators installations [61,62]. These estimations support AI decisions about the strengthening (e.g. adding generators, network expansion) of the ac network or investing in a (new or preexisting) dc network cooperating with the former to meet the targets during operation (e.g. power losses minimization, reliability improvement) [63]. Expert systems have been used for power system planning for a long time [64]. Recent works in planning mainly focus on the use of deep learning for load and RPG power forecasting [65]. This is mainly due to the need to support the power system planning with estimations of potential pitfalls in power system operations, even when the latter is AI-supported. However, there are different actors (power plants' owners, TSO, DSO, and so on) and planning levels with short- and long-term horizons that are involved in power system planning [66]. For example, decisions on scheduling power plants and fuel purchases refer to a short horizon, while decisions on investing and decommissioning power plants refer to a long horizon. Other long-term decisions refer to the time scheduling and location of new generator installations, as well as the transmission and distribution network expansion. Strengthening the power system's reliability and resilience is an important aspect that must be considered at the planning stage, as well as the advantages and drawbacks of introducing new technologies [67,68]. Given a power system based on RPGs only, these decisions are fundamental for a fast and socially-friendly transition towards SEE.AI-based holistic planning of the power system is a key brick of sustainable resource management defined by the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, that should account for environmental and socio-economic viability, and technical feasibility, thus determining what, when, and how natural resources are developed, produced, consumed, reused and recycled by society [73]. Although some studies move in this direction [74], such AI-based holistic planning aiming at implementing a power system fully based on RPGs has not been fully investigated. Moreover, the AI application for supporting sustainability at the planning stage is usually limited to the integration of RPGs only. Instead, a power system view of the sustainability vs. energy production tradeoff is essential to compare different planning choices.Solar PV technologies will dominate the renewables sector in a few years [84]. The first generation is mainly based on monocrystalline and polycrystalline silicon, and gallium arsenide. The second generation consists of amorphous silicon and thin film solar cells. The third generation includes several emerging technologies, but some solutions are at the prototyping stage only. Currently, the heterojunction bifacial panel technology is the most advanced solution that has reached the market [99]. The fourth generation (e.g. inorganic-in-organics) is at the prototyping stage, but like previous generations, its goal is to reach concurrently lower cost and higher efficiency of previous generations [100]. PV generators can present different panel arrangements and include a dc/dc converter and eventually an ESS (e.g. a battery bank), while a dc/ac converter is necessary for grid interfacing. An additional essential task of the converters' control is Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) to maximize the production. The high-frequency operation of the converters also enables the adoption of small transformers inside the conversion system. In this way, galvanic insulation is guaranteed while saving materials [101]. Although there is no concern about solar energy availability and sustainability, solar RPGs present sustainability issues that must be properly considered for exploiting the AI's ability to support SEE Ref. [102].AI has been especially used for improving the performance of the latest solar generation technologies: for supporting the research of new solutions in terms of materials, fabrication processes, and so on. ML techniques have been employed to predict the design and efficiency of solar cells before the prototyping stage. For example, they enable the optimal selection of materials for the fabrication of substrate, dye sensitizer, semiconductor, electrolyte, and catalyst for achieving high-performance dye-sensitized solar cells [103]. ML is also a catalyst in the process of new high-performance photoactive material discovery for organic solar cells [104]. In such a contest, evolutionary algorithms have also been adopted for improving modeling and performing the optimal choice among a large number of combinations [105].AI has been adopted for identifying novel materials to improve battery properties [130] and to apply LCA to enhance their sustainability, which is a key hotspot for the sustainable development of ESSs that effectively support sustainable electrical energy production [129]. MHAs and ML techniques have been used to determine the optimal modeling and sizing of energy storage units considering different optimization objectives [131]. In view of sustainability, FOMs like the ones in equations (3) and (4) can be used to guide the AI choices. The numerator will change according to the material recyclability and environmental impact along the ESS life cycle. The additional E3 can be approximately (overestimation that neglects the energy used from extracting raw material for ESS manufacturing to ESS disposal) the esteemed energy provided by the ESS, which is strongly affected by the applications that can be very diversified (from backup supply in stand-alone power systems to RPGs\u2019 power output smoothness in transmission/distribution networks). The combination of different RPG technologies supported by ESSs represents a good solution to face power output variability, but it involves different planning and operation issues, which are part of the holistic planning and management of the network. AI is especially useful for these hybrid systems, but, as in the previous cases, in the related works, the environmental impact mitigation is limited to the use of RPGs without any overall LCA guidance that enables holistic SEE Ref. [132].Power electronics is also in this case the enabler of efficiency maximization and the proper transformation of the electrical quantities (mainly the voltage level and frequency). Moreover, ESSs are fundamental in any transportation sector and are even more and more integrated in residential, commercial, and industrial loads. Therefore, power electronics converters and ESSs are key technologies for both sustainable electrical energy production and consumption. Even in this case, AI could support their sustainability, but it has been rarely used considering this target. A frequent reason behind this shortcoming is that power electronics converters and ESSs are often considered sustainable technologies per se, given that their features facilitate the green transition, without considering that they also affect the environment, which must be considered to strive for a holistic SEE. An example of their ability to act as a green transition enabler in combination with AI is the use of neural network-controlled forward boost converter-based switch-mode-power-supplies to achieve power quality improvement and voltage regulation as the grid and load conditions change [146]. Actually, the application of AI to face power electronic converter issues has been the main topic [147], while the impact on sustainability is marginally considered because only efficiency targets have been adopted [148]. As a matter of fact, facing power quality issues, such as reducing the harmonics passing through the power lines, reduces the network power losses and enables greater power delivery [140], but the consequent energy saving is not sufficient for full sustainability, thus holistic SEE is necessary. Notwithstanding, the use of power electronic converters is necessary to increase load efficiency, thus the power quality issues must be anyway solved to benefit from their introduction. In this field, the usefulness of AI is twofold for power quality, because it facilitates issues modeling and estimation [149], which is a fundamental block of any mitigating mechanisms that, in turn, can be enhanced by AI-driven approaches [146,147]. Energy saving is also the only target adopted in buildings, where, for example, AI can support home energy-saving mechanisms employing standby power reduction [150].Efficiency is the main target of these studies, while other sustainability concerns are not handled. Similarly, efficient management of energy consumption is the only target considered for AI applications that accounts for sustainability [156]. As a matter of fact, as in the previous analyses, the improvement of efficiency is not pushed by the sustainability target (but, for example, by cost reduction purposes), while the use of EVs is considered per se as the sustainability target because they contribute to reducing emissions. For the same reasons, a holistic application of AI for full SEE that accounts for LCA is neglected, thus it is necessary to use FOMs, as the ones discussed before, to guide the AI [157]. Although a few efforts have been made in this direction by some works that have addressed the critical aspects and benefits of AI in improving battery recycling within a circular economy framework that supports sustainability, other aspects must also be considered [158]. These aspects can be optimally handled by AI, as aforementioned for the RPGs. They include new sustainable materials and treatment processes; the design for recyclability, and, more in general, design for sustainability; the condition monitoring, maintenance, repairing, and end-of-life management.The variable power output of solar and wind RPG could lead to momentary excessive power supply, thus power curtailment (e.g. inverter control passes from MPPT mode to curtailment) or power shedding of a portion or the overall plant is necessary. Reducing these occurrences increases sustainability because E3 increases. The SG resources are in situ and dispersed ESSs, DR, and EVs charging (full transportation in a visionary view). These resources, together with the generators, can be managed by AI to limit these occurrences while ever reducing network losses, thus increasing E3. However, the AI choice also affects the FOMs numerators since the number of charge/discharge cycles and the way they occur could affect the lifetime of ESSs and EV batteries. The first task that AI can handle is the accurate prediction of wind and solar power curtailments in the absence of any countermeasure [166]. In this case, ML has been useful in predicting both (very) short-time power generation and load demand [65,167]. MHAs are useful to support the SG in optimally operating ESS, DR, and EVs under normal conditions with different constraints and scenarios, to face the stochastic nature of solar and wind RPGs [76]. In this way, many different targets or combinations of them can be researched. The typical target refers to operating cost minimization, while the constraints pertain to regulation limitations as well as technical limits and reliability issues [76]. However, in order to avoid limiting the SG sustainability at RPG integration, some targets specific to sustainability improvement could also be adopted.In summary, the SG has emerged as the bridge between AI and sustainable power systems because AI can exploit the SG features to improve the SG's ability to integrate RPGs and, more generally, support SEE production, delivery, and consumption. SG must accomplish the primary target of meeting the load while satisfying the power quality constraints, but among the countless ways to fulfill the target, AI is the best speed-up tool for finding the most sustainable way.

Funding Texts: Funding text 1: The \u201Csource-source\u201D model combines the stable resources in the park with the volatile WT and PV resources, which uses flexible resources to improve the stability of the comprehensive energy system. The \u201Csource-network\u201D mode is used to store the rich energy in the IES through the inertia of the transmission network, such as heat network and gas network. The \u201Csource-storage\u201D mode temporarily stores surplus energy through various energy storage methods such as heat storage tanks, gas storage tanks, energy storage batteries and pumped storage. The \u201Csource-load\u201D mode is to realize the off-peak energy use of the load by adjusting the working time and working mode of the load. Extensive research has been conducted on the coordinated operation of multiple flexible resources in energy systems. As summarized in Table 1, four primary cooperation modes have been established, with a particular focus on APs, where the integration of agriculture-specific flexible resources enables unique multi-energy synergies. APs demonstrate distinctive advantages in flexible resource coordination compared to industrial/commercial parks: abundant biomass from crop residues and livestock manure serves as a dispatchable renewable source for both short-term power compensation (e.g., biomass boiler) and seasonal energy storage (e.g., straw stockpiling) [44]. Inherent agricultural seasonality creates natural synergies - summer biogas production aligns with PV surplus while winter biomass utilization compensates for renewable deficits [12]. APs possess inherent advantages in bioenergy development,in contrast to industrial parks that depend on internally generated organic waste for biofuel production, which often requiring supplemental procurement of residual biomass or even food crops [45]. Residential areas face further limitations, where RES is constrained to rooftop photovoltaic installations, and biomass sources are restricted to non-storable municipal waste, lacking the long-term energy storage capacity characteristic of agricultural biomass [9].The selection of energy equipment and energy storage equipment in agricultural parks is constrained by the following four factors: (1) economic constraints, as some technologies involve high upfront and operational costs; (2) system compatibility and control complexity, since integrating multiple types of devices increases management difficulty; (3) spatial and environmental limitations, such as geographic requirements for pumped hydro or safety needs for hydrogen storage; and (4) policy and market mechanisms, where varying subsidy support affects investment incentives.To construct the APIES model, it is essential to integrate a wide range of external data sources. This involves developing a mathematical model that approximates the physical system, incorporating objective functions and constraints based on equipment parameters, pricing data, climatic factors, and operational costs. Depending on different classification criteria, modeling approaches are generally categorized into three main types: (1) data-deterministic modeling, (2) structure-based modeling, and (3) heuristic and AI-based optimization methods. First, based on whether the input data is deterministic, optimization methods can be classified into Deterministic Optimization and Uncertainty Optimization\u2014the latter encompassing approaches such as Stochastic Optimization (SO), Robust Optimization (RO), and Scenario-based Optimization. Second, according to whether the objective functions and constraints are linear, optimization models can be categorized as Linear Programming (LP), Nonlinear Programming (NLP), Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), and Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP). Third, Heuristic and AI-based optimization algorithms include methods such as Genetic Algorithms (GA), Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Imperialist Competitive Algorithm (ICA), and Reinforcement Learning (RL). Funding Texts: Funding text 1: Bibliometric reviews in recent years indicate that only a handful of studies have examined the spatiotemporal distribution patterns of renewable-energy sustainability in sub-Saharan Africa, underscoring an urgent need over the past decade to comprehensively map the region's sustainability trajectories [28,29]. High-resolution techno-economic-energy models emphasize Africa's potential to leapfrog conventional carbon-intensive pathways via renewables, while also demonstrating that this potential hinges on the temporal dynamics of resource availability and demand growth. For example, Neher et al. conducted an in-depth analysis of the spatiotemporal distribution and trends of solar-irradiance resources in West Africa using 1983\u20132017 satellite data, finding that daily average irradiance in the Sahara and Sahel increases by up to 5 W m\u22122 per decade, whereas southern regions exhibit a declining trend [30]. H\u00F6rsch and Calitz, using the PyPSA-ZA model for full-time co-optimization of wind and photovoltaic investments and operations in South Africa, found that up to 70 % renewable-energy penetration can be achieved\u2014with only a 20 % increase in overall system cost\u2014through flexible gas generation and transmission network expansion [31]. Gudo et al. employed GIS-based spatiotemporal suitability analysis in Jubek State, South Sudan, to identify that 62 % of the land is suitable for PV deployment, with an annual generation potential exceeding 6.05 \u00D7 109 kWh, thereby providing empirical support for local energy planning [32]. Oyewo et al., leveraging a high-resolution spatiotemporal economic model, proposed a \u201Ctrue zero-emission\u201D pathway for all of Africa, emphasizing the critical role of integrated PV\u2013storage\u2013green hydrogen systems in an economically and climatically sustainable transition [24].Nonetheless, because the dimensionality-reduction mechanism of PP and the clustering operations of FCI engage in highly nonlinear interactions, their fusion produces an inherently nonlinear optimization challenge that necessitates a suitable algorithmic strategy. Compared with traditional optimizers such as simulated annealing, particle swarm optimization, and ant colony optimization, the real-coded heuristic algorithm RAGA exhibits significant advantages [ 102\u2013105]. Its core features include a more succinct parameter configuration that circumvents the technical challenges of complex binary coding, while simultaneously addressing common issues of low global optimization efficiency and premature convergence. These attributes not only enhance the algorithm's optimization efficacy but also enable it to obtain satisfactory solutions more efficiently in practical applications, demonstrating strong adaptability and usability. Juan and Chen combined the RAGA-PP and KL-TOPSIS methods to assess urban flood resilience and optimize indicator weights [106]. Ji et al. applied a projection pursuit evaluation model based on a real-coded accelerating genetic algorithm to assess wetland soil quality [107]. Shu et al. used RAGA in a projection pursuit classification (PPC) model to support real estate investment decision-making [108]. Su et al. conducted a comparative assessment of the RAGA-PP framework's reliability against three benchmark evaluation techniques\u2014entropy-weighted TOPSIS, rank-sum ratio, and principal component analysis\u2014within the context of WRCC assessments for the HREEB. Their results demonstrated that the RAGA-PP model produced the greatest differentiation index, indicating superior reliability in this application [109]. More broadly, by virtue of its powerful search capabilities and streamlined computational design, the RAGA algorithm has been successfully applied across numerous domains to tackle complex nonlinear optimization problems while reducing computational burden.According to Fig. 6, the 35 African countries exhibited marked dynamic evolution between 2014 and 2023. During 2014\u20132016, Evaluation Level 1 dominated, as most countries were still in the stage of constructing energy policy frameworks and paid relatively little attention to renewable energy development. In 2017\u20132019, a clear divergence emerged: industrially stronger countries such as Egypt, South Africa, and Morocco took the lead. South Africa, leveraging the REIPPPP, increased its photovoltaic (PV) installations, and concentrated solar power plant in Morocco's Noor achieved 400 MW of commercial operation. By contrast, sub-Saharan countries such as Niger and Burkina Faso remained at Level 1 due to shortages of technical personnel and weak grid infrastructure, highlighting regional development imbalances. The year 2020 marked a pivotal turning point, as inflows of international climate finance drove a significant uplift in overall levels, laying the groundwork for subsequent breakthroughs. In 2021\u20132022, Africa's overall national renewable energy sustainability remained low, and the COVID-19 pandemic led to delays in many renewable energy projects. International energy price volatility induced policy swings in fossil-energy-dependent countries, while drought in East Africa undermined the supply stability of hydropower-dominated systems. Yet these crises also spurred transformation: the Africa Green Hydrogen Alliance was officially launched, promoting green hydrogen transitions in six countries. The World Bank invested USD 311 million in West Africa to support pilot projects, although local industrial chains and financing mechanisms have yet to mature. By 2023, most countries were classified as \u201CStrong Sustainability\u201D or \u201CGeneral Sustainability,\u201D with few in the weak-sustainability category. Breakthroughs in regional grid interconnection and declining PV technology costs drove wider adoption. China-Africa cooperation projects accounted for 38 percent of new developments\u2014for example, the 50 MW Garissa PV plant now supplies electricity to some 380,000 people. Current challenges center on financing gaps, insufficient technology localization, and delayed climate-adaptation capacity building, but the USD 1.3 trillion annual climate-finance target established at COP29 provides momentum for Africa to accelerate clean energy project deployment. Funding Texts: Funding text 1: Achieving optimal power operation and management requires addressing the inherent unpredictability of solar power systems. This exploration is essential for enhancing overall efficiency and stability. Historical time-series data play a pivotal role in formulating high-performance power prediction methodologies, as evidenced by recent studies highlighting the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques, particularly in the realm of solar power prediction (Succetti et al., 2020). The evolution of AI has spurred the development of diverse applications, with a notable emphasis on solar power prediction. Advancements in machine learning and deep learning have demonstrated proficiency in capturing intricate nonlinear properties (Ahmed et al., 2020; D\u00EDaz-Bedoya et al., 2023; Suanpang and Jamjuntr, 2024). Traditional AI approaches, including support vector machines (SVMs) and neural networks (Meenal and Selvakumar, 2018; Yang et al., 2023; Anupong et al., 2023), are used to elucidate complex interactions within time-series data. The persistence model is a common statistical baseline for predicting solar power. Although these models perform well with simple data and smooth applications, they suffer from the complexity of historical solar power time-series data affected by variable weather conditions. For instance, the autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) model yields weak results (Zhou et al., 2021; Sharadga et al., 2020; Szostek et al., 2024). To address these challenges, deep learning models such Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are commonly used (Wang et al., 2020; Kothona et al., 2023; Ghimire et al., 2022a), specifically CXGBRFR framework (Ghimire et al., 2022b). However, PV power data involves both temporal and spatial aspects. CNNs excel at capturing spatial features, while RNNs and long short-term memory (LSTM) specialize in handling temporal aspects, indicating a gap in their joint capabilities. To address this gap, several hybrid models, such as LSTM-CNN (Aksan et al., 2023; Jalali et al., 2022; Marinho et al., 2022), ICEEMDAN-DRESNET (Ghimire et al., 2022c), ConvLSTM-BDGRU (Khan et al., 2023a), CNN-LSTM (Lim et al., 2022; Alharkan et al., 2023; Al-Ali et al., 2023), PCA-GWO-GRNN (Ge et al., 2020), KRR (Deo et al., 2023), CMPL (Ghimire et al., 2023), wavelet pattern decomposition with ConvLSTM (Obiora and Ali, 2021; Costa, 2022; Hu et al., 2024), and advanced LSTM (Ahmed et al., 2022; Gupta and Singh, 2023; Jailani et al., 2023; Al-Jaafreh et al., 2022), have been developed. These hybrid models adeptly leverage the strengths of CNNs and RNNs, demonstrating considerable promise for PV power prediction. An innovative vanilla transformer (VTx) model has recently surfaced for sequence-to-sequence modeling (Zhou et al., 2023; Dong et al., 2023). Originally tailored for natural language processing, its applications have extended to computer vision (Wang et al., 2018; Travieso-Gonz\u00E1lez et al., 2024; Paletta et al., 2023). And represent a novel direction of research (Posp\u00EDchal et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2021).The performance of decision trees has become evident in the exploration of traditional models. With an MSE of 0.1142 and an MAE of 0.1967, the decision trees outperformed several other models, showing resilience and adaptability. Conversely, the intricacies of the data were addressed by applying linear regression and support vector regression (SVR). The elevated mean square error (MSE) values of 1.9731 and 2.3099 emphasize the difficulties encountered by these models in capturing the inherent nonlinear relationships in PV power generation. The associated mean absolute errors (MAEs) corroborate this observation, revealing average deviations of 121.02% for linear regression and 115.17% for support vector regression (SVR). Funding Texts: Funding text 1: The authors would like to acknowledge the National Science Foundation under Grant 2220347 and Grant 2145408 , the US Department of Energy under award DE-CR0000018 and award DE-EE0009658 , and grants from Princeton University\u2019s School of Engineering and Applied Science and Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment , for their support of this work.; Funding text 2: The DataGuard Energy Data Privacy Program (DataGuard) released by the U.S. Department of Energy\u2019s Office of Electricity [194] addresses the associated privacy concerns between utilities, consumers, and vendors. It requires a comprehensive approach to enhancing consumers\u2019 security, tackling identity theft, and improving privacy. The reviewed comprehensive privacy preservation techniques hold huge potential for addressing privacy challenges in pilot DER projects at scale. In what follows, we give some real-world DER projects that encounter privacy concerns. The U.S.\u2019s Xcel Energy Wind and Solar Program [195] integrates renewables for consumers to offset carbon footprints. It involves collecting detailed operational data from consumers that can raise risks of unauthorized access to sensitive generation and consumption patterns. The flagship Horizon Europe Program funded by the European Union [196] , which emphasizes smart grid integration of DERs and citizen-led initiatives (e.g., community energy projects). Privacy breaches in data management and sharing among different stakeholders can increase the risks of customer data misuse. Another example is the U.K.\u2019s Open Networks Project [197] , which aims to harmonize DER visibility information through consistent data flow from DERs to distribution network operators. The project addresses the potential privacy breaches associated with the exposure of DER data during information exchange between stakeholders, necessitating the adoption of privacy-preserving and scalable information exchange structures reviewed in the paper. ; Funding text 3: The authors would like to acknowledge the National Science Foundation, USA under Grant 2220347 and Grant 2145408, the US Department of Energy under award DE-CR0000018 and award DE-EE0009658, and grants from Princeton University's School of Engineering and Applied Science, USA and Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment, USA, for their support of this work.

For instance, the accuracy of integration in the frequency domain undermines the effectiveness of FFT and IFFT, which usually correlates with the length of the transformed signal. For online signals, the ideal length of the transformed signal should be equal to the number of transient monitoring points, resulting in inaccurate cut-off frequency and weight parameters for HPF, LPF and LSSVM. Funding Texts: Funding text 1: In the realm of energy management strategies for DFR, numerous experts and researchers have delved deep into this kind of topic. Various projects and practical applications have shed light on the potential of DFR. In the United States, the predominant approach to managing distributed resources revolves around demand response(DR), like the Brooklyn Microgrid Project [ 9 ]. Meanwhile, Japan's efforts are showcased through the smart community demonstration project in Hokkaido, emphasizing advancements in smart communications and decentralized energy systems [ 10 ]. Additionally, the RESPOND project in Spain [ 11 ], supported by the EU's H2020 program, introduced an energy automation control tool. This tool integrates both supply and demand considerations, ensuring real\u2010time optimal energy regulation. From a technical perspective, current research on DFR regulation strategies mostly focuses on utilizing optimization techniques, which include mixed integer linear programming (MILP) [ 12 ], model predictive control (MPC) [ 13 ], game theory solutions [ 14, 15 ], stochastic optimization [ 16 ], and robust optimization [ 17 ]. Reference [ 18 ] considered the uncertainty of distributed power sources and proposed a two\u2010stage optimization model based on distributed robust optimization (DRO) to study the energy management strategy of DFRs in data centre. In work [ 19 ], researchers constructed a multi\u2010objective intraday rolling scheduling model and proposed a time\u2010varying iterative solution method to guide the operational decision\u2010making of BESS. It's worth noting that the basic theory of optimization methods leads to these optimization strategies predominantly rely on model\u2010based control frameworks. However, it is difficult to form an accurate physical model and efficiently control the demand\u2010side resources. Moreover, most optimization methods are aimed at regulating resources for day\u2010ahead or intraday timelines, yet they fall short in responding to data in real\u2010time environments. Hence, a significant hurdle still remains in accurately modelling and regulating flexibility resources at the distribution network (DN) level, which brings about problems of high computational complexity and low level of intelligent decision\u2010making. ; Funding text 2: This work is supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant No. 52107079, Natural Science Foundation of Jiangsu Province under Grant No. BK20210243, Young Elite Scientists Sponsorship Program by Jiangsu Association for Science and Technology (JSTJ\u20102023\u2010XH050) and \u201CZhishan Youth Scholar\u201D Program of Southeast University under Grant No.2242023R40048.

Funding Texts: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) were investigated by Raj et al. (2018) for the purpose of fault detection in asymmetric multilevel inverters. This study exemplifies the adaptability of machine learning methodologies, since it demonstrates the ability to identify faults in asymmetric inverters [36]. In diagnostic procedures, their results indicate that artificial neural networks (ANNs) have the potential to properly diagnose problems and minimize reaction times. The authors Wang et al. (2016) developed a technique for defect detection that was based on support vector machines (SVM), the fast Fourier transform (FFT), and the robust principal component analysis (RPCA) [37]. A considerable improvement in defect detection accuracy is achieved with the use of both frequency domain and statistical approaches, as shown by this integrated methodology. An improved support vector machine approach that was augmented by a gray wolf optimization algorithm was suggested by Yuan et al. (2023) for the purpose of detecting faults in H-bridge cascaded five-level inverters [38]. According to the results of their investigation, improving the settings of the support vector machine (SVM) using the gray wolf algorithm results in improved generalization over a wide range of operating situations and a greater level of accuracy in defect identification. Ali and colleagues (2021) conducted a study to investigate the utilization of machine learning techniques for the purpose of identifying open switch faults in cascade H-bridge multi-level inverters that are used in distributed power producers [39]. The research demonstrates that machine learning is an excellent method for tackling real-time fault diagnostic difficulties, and it also highlights the usefulness of this method in practical contexts.This work was supported by the Researchers Supporting Project number (RSP2024R258), King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Funding Texts: Funding text 1: The authors would like to thank the funding support from the Kempe Foundation (Kempestiftelserna) for Grant number JCK22-0025, Sweden. ; Funding text 2: The paper investigates the application of machine learning (ML) for voltage sag source localization (VSSL) in electrical power systems. To overcome feature-selection challenges for traditional ML methods and provide more meaningful sequential features for deep learning methods, the paper proposes three time-sample-based feature forms, and evaluates an existing feature form. The effectiveness of these feature forms is assessed using k-means clustering with k = 2 referred to as downstream and upstream classes, according to the direction of voltage sag origins. Through extensive voltage sag simulations, including noises in a regional electrical power network, k-means identifies a sequence involving the multiplication of positive-sequence current magnitude with the sine of its angle as the most prominent feature form. The study develops further traditional ML methods such as decision trees (DT), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), k-nearest neighbor (KNN), an ensemble learning (EL), and a designed one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN). The results found that the combination of 1D-CNN or SVM with the most prominent feature achieved the highest accuracies of 99.37% and 99.13%, respectively, with acceptable/fast prediction times, enhancing VSSL. The exceptional performance of the CNN was also approved by field measurements in a real power network. However, selecting the best ML methods for deployment requires a trade-off between accuracy and real-time implementation requirements. The research findings benefit network operators, large factory owners, and renewable energy park producers. They enable preventive maintenance, reduce equipment downtime/damage in industry and electrical power systems, mitigate financial losses, and facilitate the assignment of power-quality penalties to responsible parties.The authors would like to thank the funding support from the Kempe Foundation (Kempestiftelserna) for Grant number JCK22-0025, Sweden. This work has been also supported by the ARIS under Project P2-0115, Slovenia.

Funding Details: Whale Optimization Algorithm
Funding Texts: Energy management strategy (EMS) of microgrids is categorized as DELD according to the minimization of the costs, being more complex than SELD. Distributed energy resources (DERs) are composed of fossil-fueled generators, renewable energy sources (RES), e.g., micro-turbines, fuel cells, energy storage systems (ESS), e.g., battery and flywheel, etc. (Zheng et al., 2018). Microgrid can therefore be considered as the DERs coupled with the load demand points in a certain geographical area (Ghasemi and Enayatzare, 2018; Anestis and Georgios, 2019). It can operate as utility connected or islanded but utility connected ones have more reliability and efficiency due to the possibility of buy/sell option from utility. The utility connected DER can rely on the grid for support during unexpected shut down of the network. This has invited immense research interest in this domain of microgrid energy management. References (Chen et al., 2011) and (Kasaei, 2018) employed Imperialist Competitive Algorithm and Matrix Real Coded Genetic Algorithm to minimize the generation cost of a grid-connected microgrid. Numerous case studies were considered by authors to analyze the algorithm's ability for tackling narrow operating range of DERs, load variation and erratic electricity pricing. Authors in (Basu and Chowdhury, 2013) have established cuckoo Search Algorithm as a better performing technique when contrsted with Differential Evolution and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). An islanded microgrid system installed with two wind turbines is accounted for DELD problem by modeling on the basis of wind speed. The authors in (Moghaddam et al., 2011) applied an Adaptive Modified PSO for generating economic dispatch solution in an utility-connected microgrid. The authors in (Rabiee et al., 2018) provided equal footing to economic and emission dispatch as objectives to be analysed using a Modified Imperialist Competitive Algorithm.Emission dispatch and combined economic emission dispatch (CEED) were evaluated by authors in references (Trivedi et al., 2018; Elattar, 2018; Dey et al., 2019) employing Interior Search Algorithm, Modified Harmony Search Algorithm and Whale Optimization Algorithm, respectively, on a 3 unit islanded microgrid system supported with photovoltaic (PV) and wind system. Numerous price penalty factors were calculated, evaluated and the minimal value of all was chosen to perform CEED. References (Kumar et al., 2016; Gholami and Dehnavi, 2019; Askarzadeh, 2017) used Artificial Fish Swarm Algorithm, Modified Personal Best PSO and Memory-based Genetic Algorithm, respectively, on an islanded microgrid system consisting 3 WTs, 2 PV systems and a CHP connected to IEEE 37-node feeder. Modified Personal Best PSO provided the least cost among the three. Enhancing the load demand by 10% of the prevailing value, authors in (Ramli et al., 2019) studied unilateral power flow for two scenarios of a microgrid connected to utility and energy storage apparatus. Many authors have performed research for optimal scheduling of Energy Storage System (ESS) and DERs with a prime intent of generation cost minimization applying Improved Bat Algorithm (Bahmani-Firouzi and Azizipanah-Abarghooee, 2014), Quasi-Oppositional Swine Influenza Model-based Optimization (Sharma et al., 2018a), GWO (Sharma et al., 2016) and Whale Optimization Algorithm (Sharma et al., 2018b). Minimization of cost of generation for an integrated renewable system comprising of small and huge microgrid is executed by authors in (Dey et al., 2020) applying CSA. It was observed that CSA excelled in performance contrasted with numerous metaheuristics in cost minimization problem of microgrid. The authors in (Mirjalili et al., 2014) established a new algorithm based on the hunting pattern of grey wolves and a modified approach of this algorithm was proposed by authors in (Khandelwal et al., 2018). Another approach of utilizing sine and cosine function in optimization is proposed by authors in (Mirjalili, 2016). The authors in (Askarzadeh, 2016) applied Crow Search Algorithm for solving complex optimization issues. The CEC2011 has been utilized by authors to test the robustness of evolutionary algorithms in (Das and Suganthan, 2010). The authors in (Rizk-Allah et al., 2018) incorporated chaotic approach to the CSA algorithm to enhance its potency. The authors in (Kumar and Saravanan, 2019) provided a detailed research study with respect to day ahead scheduling of a microgrid and energy storae system. A comprehensive research analysis on non-parametric statistical approach for establishing the difference between swarm intelligence and evolutionary algorithms is presented in (Derrac et al., 2011) whereas numerous parametric and non-parametric statistical procedures is evaluated in (Sheskin, 2020).

Funding Details: Energy Policy and Planning Office, EPPO; Ministry of Higher Education, Malaysia, MOHE; Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka, UTeM, (FRGS/1/2018/TK04/UTEM/02/5); Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka, UTeM
Funding Texts: Funding text 1: The authors gratefully acknowledge the Ministry of Higher Education Malaysia and Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka for supporting this research through research grant FRGS/1/2018/TK04/UTEM/02/5 .; Funding text 2: According to a market overview report [ 196 ], the energy storage market of the ASEAN region is predicted to achieve USD 4.24 billion by 2027. Due to the increasing demand for reliable electricity supply in both residential as well as commercial sectors, BESS is most likely to be the preferred option to boost the market expansion in the ASEAN region. The Energy Plan of Philippines 2012–2030 has aimed to implement ES for integrating renewable energy into the network. The government of Philippines aims to install solar PV with a total capacity of 15.29 GW by 2030, subsequently increasing the demand of BESS for solar rooftops in the country [ 197 , 198 ]. In 2021, the first utility-scale battery with a capacity of 20 MW for grid stabilization in Kabankalan, Philippines was commissioned by Fluence and is now in active service [ 199 ]. Indonesia is further behind their neighboring countries, such as The Philippines, in ES projects development. Indonesia aims to electrify the isolated communities across the archipelago nation. The national energy policy of Indonesia has set a 31 % renewable energy source target by 2050, where Indonesia has the potential to produce more than 207 GW from solar generation [ 200 ]. According to the Indonesian Power Industry Survey [ 201 ], the electrification of remote communities can be achieved by implementing a mini grid with ES technology. The World Bank authorized a loan of USD 380 million to develop Indonesia's first pump storage hydropower project with an anticipated capacity of 1040 MW located between Jakarta and Bandung in 2021 [ 202 ]. In the next year, Quantum Power Asia and Ib Vogt solar developers are planning to build a PV plant with ES (3.5 GW, 12 GW h) in Riau, Indonesia to provide electricity to Singapore via subsea cable [ 203 ]. The government of Thailand has shown determination to address blackout and issues of the grid through the Power Development Plan 2015–2036. A research grant with USD 23 million in research fund was provided by the Energy Policy and Planning Office to promote the development of ES in Thailand with different research frameworks, which focus on application and research development [ 204 ]. Sungrow and Super Energy plan to build a BESS project with a capacity of 45 MW/136.24 MW h in Thailand in 2022. This project is expected to provide clean electricity and improve the stability of the grid in Thailand [ 205 ]. A pilot BESS project in Mae Hong Son was conducted by the Provincial Electricity Authority and Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand to explore the use of BESS to provide support for power outage event; however, the project is yet to be in operation [ 206 ]. A target of 200 MW of ESS to be deployed beyond 2025 has been set by Singapore in its first ESS Technology Roadmap report [ 207 ]. The first utility-scale ESS of Singapore was deployed at a substation in Woodlands to maintain stable power supply through solar generation and power more than 200 four-room Housing Board households for a day. Singapore will deploy its first floating storage pilot project with capacity of 7.5 MW/7.5 MW h, where the testbed will utilize seawater to cool the battery cells of the system [ 208 , 209 ]. In Vietnam, the total power demand is predicted to have an increment of 10 % per year. According to the report of Electricity of Vietnam, a power shortage of 13.3 billion kWh in 2023 is estimated, where BESS is selected to be the solution for this shortage by the National Power Transmission Corporation of Vietnam [ 210 ]. A pilot utility-scale BESS with capacity of 7.5 MW/15 MW h will be launched by AC Energy and the renewable energy platform of Vietnam in Khanh Hoa province following a USD 2.96 million grant approved by the Consulate of the US. The project is expected to identify the technical and economic capabilities of ES to maximize the efficiency and reliability of renewable energy [ 211 ]. It can be noticed that ASEAN countries are starting to implement ES pilot projects; however, most ASEAN countries do not include ES policy or incentives for ESS. As in Malaysia, the lack of incentives for solar PV with ESS is the shortcoming of the latest NEM 3.0 program. The priority for ASEAN countries is to identify the benefits of ESS to apply a suitable policy with more pilot projects.

Funding Texts: Ever since the industrial revolution and urbanization, a steep increase in the energy demand has put the electricity market highly competitive in developing technologies to meet the substantial energy requirement preserving the potential social, economic, and environmental impacts. However conventional fossil fuel-based power generation has led to severe environmental impacts like global warming and subsequent deterioration in biodiversity. In efforts to reduce the greenhouse gas emission and carbon footprint, most countries have taken a worldwide perspective of upgrading their energy sector with potential RES as a sound alternative to the conventional sources. Decarbonizing the energy sector and supporting global initiatives to curtail global warming are highly crucial in the current scenario. Wind energy being a clearly in-exhaustive clean renewable source has drawn an accelerated penetration level in the existing electrical power system in recent years. With 837 GW of global wind power capacity now in 2022, the world will be able to avoid more than 1.2 billion tons of CO2 every year [1]. But due to the intermittent character of wind speed, the power system has become more unreliable with the increased integration of wind power into the existing power system. This crucial problem draws the attention of many researchers in developing a computationally efficient forecast model for accurately predicting wind energy for efficient power system planning, operation management and control [2,3]. Researchers have extensively developed a variety of wind speed prediction systems over the last 20 years to increase the prediction accuracy.The wind speed data is gathered from a weather station installed at Amrita School of Engineering, Bengaluru with funding provided by the VGST -Vision Group of Science and Technology, Government of Karnataka, India (K-FIST (Level-1) GRD number: 671).

Funding Texts: Funding text 1: Sparrow search algorithm (SSA) [49] is an innovative meta-heuristic optimization algorithm founded on group foraging and anti-predation behavior of sparrows by Xue and Shen in 2020. SSA has been highly regarded by numerous researchers [ 50–52] for its benefits of better search accuracy, quick convergence speed and ease of escaping local optimal solutions. Simultaneously, many scholars have improved SSA to enhance its output further and design more algorithmic versions to solve practical engineering problems. Yuan et al. [53] employed the barycentric reverse learning mechanism in population initialization to improve local search performance, particularly for the optical voltage microgrid system. Ouyang et al. [54] introduced sine and cosine search methods to escape local optimization. Their results demonstrated that the SSA can significantly resolve the problem of support vector machine parameter optimization. Wang et al. [55] integrated the PSO and SSA algorithms to create a hybrid algorithm named PESSA, which performed exceptionally well in UAV path planning problems. These engineering examples validate that, compared to the original algorithm, improved SSA variants offer faster convergence speed with less susceptibility to local optima. Therefore, exploring improvements to initial population or population location update methods to optimal chillers loading, could be beneficial.This research was supported by the Research Project of China Northwest Architecture Design and Research Institute Co. Funding Texts: Funding text 1: The main objectives of P2P energy sharing are to cover stochastic energy demands with high penetration of renewable energy, stabilize the grid power under integration of intermittent renewable energy supply and improve the economic performance. The underlying mechanism is to cover the demand of neighborhood buildings with surplus renewable energy in a geographically different building. The main advantages of P2P energy sharing mainly include system efficiency improvements [8], reduction in required energy storage capacity [9] and primary energy consumption [9], high renewable penetration with decreased energy loss in storage and transmission processes [10], avoidance on devaluation of energy quality and mitigated grid pressure for energy interactions [11]. P2P based electricity market design can promote the decarbonization with renewable and storage technologies [12], improve system efficiency [13], reliable trading with PV forecast error and uncertainty [14], and reduce losses, voltage support and congestion management for local power grid [15]. Simulation tools mainly include MATLAB/Simulink [16], TRNSYS [9], Python/Matlab Interface [17] and Homer [18]. In terms of the cogeneration energy sharing of surplus heat and electricity, Hirvonen et al. [9] indicated that cogeneration energy sharing strategy can reduce the required storage capacity and primary energy consumption by 1–9%. The price-based demand response strategy can guide the dynamic energy sharing with cost saving and improved PV sharing [16].With the increased deployment of distributed renewable systems and associated electricity infrastructures, P2P sharing and trading become necessary to motivate more end-users’ participation. Electricity market design can promote P2P trading with reduced reliance on power grid, and it involves multidisciplinary research and multiple efforts from system planner, operator, policy-maker and so on. P2P based electricity market design can promote the decarbonization with renewable and storage technologies [12], improve system efficiency [13], reliable trading with PV forecast error and uncertainty [14], provide loss reduction, voltage support and congestion management for local power grid [15]. Zhang et al. [15] conducted a coordinated market design to provide multiple functions such as loss reduction, voltage support and congestion management for local power grid with P2P energy trading. Depending on the roles of centralized and distributed energy storages, Lüth et al. [12] indicated that P2P trade and battery usage are critical elements that need to be considered for local electricity market. Furthermore, the possibility for reserving capacity of a centralized battery needs to be considered for market-based incentives. Parag and Sovacool [13] studied the electricity market design in respect to grid integration, P2P models and prosumer community. Results showed that the electricity market design can improve energy efficiency, democratize demand-response and promote renewable energy technologies. Cadre et al. [57] studied the impact of evolution from the variational to Generalized Nash Equilibrium on a P2P electricity market. Results showed that due to coordination, market liquidity and information asymmetry, the P2P market design shows superior performance than the classical centralized market design. Zhang et al.
