Performance Evaluation of Proposed Method To validate the performance of the proposed framework, the trained model is tested with load and PV profiles that Fig. 2. Variation of PV and load profile in every 5 minutes are distinct from the training data, and the result is compared with the base case scenario (the agents don\u2019t provide any action). An over-voltage scenario is created by adding some high-capacity PV in several nodes of the IEEE 34-bus test system. By controlling (absorbing/injecting) reactive power, smart inverters can regulate the voltage of the network. The proposed decentralized framework can optimally control the reactive power of the inverters to improve the voltage profile. Due to cloud dynamics in real-time, the PV generation output can change quickly within a few minutes or seconds. Fig. 2 shows the variation of active power generation output of all PV inverters and the variation of loads for every five minutes that is used for validating the proposed approach. Fig. 3 illustrates the amount of reactive power absorbed/injected by PV inverters to regulate the voltage within a permissible range. Fig. 4 depicts the voltage fluctuation at node-858 of the test system for both the trained model and the base case. It is observed that in the base case scenario, there is a voltage violation according to the ANSI voltage standard limit whereas no voltage violation occurs in case of the proposed model. Moreover, the variation of voltage is higher in the base case than in the proposed trained model. To further justify the robustness of the method with respect to large stochasticity, the proposed model is evaluated with a profile that varies within every ten minutes as shown in Fig. 5. Fig. 6 shows the voltage fluctuation at node-858 for both the trained model and the base case scenarios. It also shows that the proposed approach has the superior performance than the base case. Finally, Fig. 7 depicts the variation of the voltages in all 34 nodes at 20th minute for the profile shown in Fig. 2. It illustrates that the proposed trained model has an improved voltage profile than the base case in terms of voltage variation and violation. IV. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORKS This paper has proposed a centralized training and decentralized execution-based multi-agent DRL (MADRL) approach for voltage regulation in distribution systems with high penetration of PVs. The network is divided into several subnetworks and each agent is assigned to control the voltages of a sub-region. All three agents are trained centrally to learn the coordinated control strategies directed by the reward function and execute them in a decentralized manner to reduce Fig. 3. Reactive power support by PV inverters Fig. 4. Voltages at node-858 in every 5 minutes Fig. 5. Variation of PV and load profile in every 10 minutes Fig. 6. Voltages at node-858 in every 10 minutes Fig. 7. Voltages of each node at 20th minute the communication burden for real-time implementation. The proposed MADRL framework performs the real-time voltage control using the local information from each sub-region. The applicability of the proposed model was assessed with different PV and load profiles and with some drastic changes in their pattern. The performance of the proposed approach was measured in terms of amount of reduction in the voltage fluctuations and was compared with a base case scenario when agents didn\u2019t take any action. The proposed method was effectively able to coordinate between different agents to optimally control the reactive power outputs of PV inverters and to minimize the voltage fluctuation of the network. Unlike existing DRL-based VVC frameworks, the proposed approach does not depend on system modeling both training and execution phases. In a future work, generative adversarial network (GAN) will be incorporated to estimate missing/unobservable generation data of behind-the-meter PV inverters to make the proposed model highly applicable to the real-world systems. Funding Details: Artificial Neural Network; Back Propagation Neural Network; FNN, (2022); Neural Network; Recurrent Neural Network
Funding Texts: Fundamental analysis and technical analysis are the two important factors in stock market forecasting. Fundamental analysis depends upon macro-economic factors where as technical analysis depends upon historical time series data. Fundamental analysis is used for long term prediction spectrum while technical analysis is used for short term prediction like intraday, weekly, and monthly. To get more efficient result in the prediction of historical time series data researchers introduced Machine Learning (ML) techniques from last few decades. Statistical methods like Auto Regressive (AR) (Stock et al., 1988), Auto Regressive Moving Average (ARMA) (Xu, 2017), Generalized Auto Regressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) (Kristjanpoller and Minutolo, 2015), Support Vector Machine (SVM) (Mustaffa et al., 2015) and Back Propagation Neural Network (BPNN) (Yu et al., 2018) are proposed to forecast stock market price. Some researchers proposed hybrid/modified ML techniques for more accurate forecasting. Text mining and Artificial Neural Network (ANN) combined to predict gold prices by comparing with ARMA model (Chen et al., 2016). To forecast oil price a new information fusion method is proposed (Ye et al., 2019). The complicacy of ANN is overcome by Support Vector Machines (SVM) to forecast time series data (Saitta, 1995). SVM and Adaptive Neuro Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) are compared with each other in terms of finger-vein identification (Wu and Liu, 2011). As time series oil and gold prices data are non-stationary, nonlinear, and noisy, hence hybridization of decomposition methods with ML techniques can be an useful tool to get more accurate prediction. Decomposition method like Wavelet Transform (WT) combined with Adaptive Neuro Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) and Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to forecast stock market price (Chandar, 2019; Hsieh et al., 2011). The fusion of EMD with ANN, Factorization machine based Neural Network (FNN) and Support Vector Regression (SVR) are used to predict time series data (stock market price and electric load) (Lahmiri, 2020; Yaslan and Bican, 2017; Zhou et al., 2019). Researchers proposed a Complete Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise (CEEMDAN) hybridized with Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) to predict financial time series (Cao et al., 2018). Further, the decomposition methods (variational mode decomposition and improved complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise) are integrated with machine learning techniques to improve the accuracy of crude oil price prediction (Li et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2022). Plakandaras and Ji (2022) merged Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (EEMD) with SVR to enhance the accuracy of gold price prediction.

Funding Texts: Funding text 1: The Transactive approach of energy management and control was first demonstrated in the Olympic Peninsula Project [124] , which was a part of Pacific Northwest GridWise™ Testbed Demonstration Projects. The project was conducted in Washington and Oregon. It was funded by the U.S. Department of Energy and several northwest power utilities of the country. The project was initiated to investigate the potential of utilising demand-side flexibility as an alternative to capacity expansion of the capacity constraint transmission system of the region, which was forecast to be inadequate for supplying the following winter peak demand. The project adopted a real-time regional marginal electricity price and used it as an effective control signal to manage transmission and distribution congestion. The residential consumers and local DG owners would react to this price signal and bid into a local electricity market with the desired power to be consumed or supplied. A central entity would clear the market and dispatch these responsive resources according to the wholesale costs of electricity, network congestion, and customer demand. The project successfully demonstrated that passive residential loads and local DGs can be converted into active dispersed grid resources in the TE framework by using the real-time regional electricity price as an effective control signal. Project outcomes verified that the transactive management of active dispersed resources can be utilised to address network congestion instead of investing in grid reinforcement. ; Funding text 2: This work was supported in part by International Macquarie University Research Training Program scholarship , in part by the U.S. National Science Foundation under Grant ECCS-2039716 and in part by a grant from the C3.ai Digital Transformation Institute .; Funding text 3: Decentralised Energy Exchange (deX) [128] is an ongoing TE implementation project that started in 2017. It is led by an Australian energy tech startup, GreenSync, and funded by the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA). The objective of this project is to create an open marketplace to transact excess energy from rooftop PV and residential storage between consumers, businesses, communities, and network utilities. The project aims to allow consumers with renewable generation resources or storage systems to obtain incentives and lower their demand on the public grid during system peaks. To this end, it focuses on developing an online exchange platform for buying and selling electrical energy from consumer-end DERs. The Australian electricity market intends to potentially adopt a two-sided market architecture to harness new and disruptive technologies such as behind-the-meter DERs while empowering all energy system users, from small customers to large generators [72] . Therefore, the deX platform is expected to support an efficient orchestration of supply and demand entities while providing the services needed to keep the power system safe, secure, and reliable.

Funding Texts: In the past 40 years, many enterprises and institutions have launched research projects to promote the technical maturity of EMA. As early as the 1980s, the U.S. Air Force tried to use EMA on the flight control system of the C‐141 transport aircraft and studied its reliability and maintainability [ 12, 13 ]. The Electrically Powered Actuation Design (EPAD) program [ 3 ] is also launched by the U.S. military and NASA to enhance the maturity of EMA, and the fault diagnosis technology of EMA is studied preliminarily. Subsequently, many EMA DPHM projects have significantly contributed to the technical maturity of EMA. Integrated Prognostics and Health Management (IPHM) and Aircraft Electrical Power Systems Prognostics and Health Management (AEPHM) [ 14 ] are both launched to work on the EMA DPHM. With the development of aviation technology, higher requirements are put forward for the reliability of EMA. Integrated Vehicle Health Management (IVHM) [ 15 ] and the Integrated Flight Control & Actuator Health Management (IFC&AHM) [ 16 ] are launched to improve the effectiveness of DPHM methods. The ACTUATION‐2015 project [ 17 ] and the Reliable Electrical Actuation (REACT) [ 18 ] are funded by European countries to study the technology of EMA DPHM and obtain a good effect. Umbra Group Aerospace and Liebherr‐Aerospace in Lindenberg have also set up their test stands to study the EMA DPHM algorithms [ 19, 20 ]. Mazzoleni et al. [ 21 ] elaborated four research projects launched by the European Union and Italy, separately, to investigate the EMA fault diagnosis technologies. They also provide constructive remarks and advice on EMA fault diagnosis, which can be regarded as an excellent reference to study condition monitoring algorithms of EMA or build EMA experiment devices.

Funding Texts: Funding text 1: New class notations related to digital features (DNV, 2021g) have also been published to support yards in their deliveries to make ships ready to transfer data to shore including vibration and noise data for systems, equipment, and structures. E.g., the class notation D-INF for data collection infrastructure focus on network, connectivity, data quality and security management and distinguish between standardized ISO based (ISO 19487:2018/19488:2018) or proprietary solutions. This is a foundation for getting reliable data to shore for other digital features like data driven verification (DDV notation) and remote witnessing (REW notation) which are typical class activities. D-INF compliments also smart technologies supporting innovative green-or general digitalization-solutions, which goes well beyond class activities but towards the owners’ own needs or towards their clients, e.g., Smart notation (DNV, 2021h). For innovative solutions there are even assurance programs for the use case of DTs (DNV, 2020). These are examples from DNV, but other class societies support these activities with similar platforms, services, rules or standards, e.g., ABS, NK, LR and BV. Rødseth & Berre (2018) proposed “Maritime Data Space” (MDS), a conceptual general framework adapted for the maritime world, capable to host and interconnect subsystems and processes focusing on ships. MDS replicates a concept called “Industrial Data Space” (IDS) developed within the Industry 4.0 framework for land-based industry. In 1998, Heath and Imregun first gave a comparative survey of vibration analysis methods for interpreting measured data at turbo-machinery rotor blade tips by using optical laser probes [26] . After then, many new studies continued to be done to promote the development of the BTT technique. Also the authors have carried out deep investigations on BTT-based vibration monitoring under support provided by the National Basic Research Program of China. However, there are still many issues in engineering applications to be solved. Thus it is very significant to review and summarize the BTT technique. The main purpose of this paper tries to summarize main challenges, review present progress and discuss future directions. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. History and basic principle of the BTT technique is outlined in Section 2 . Then Section 3 summarizes three main challenges in the BTT technique for blade health monitoring. In Sections 4 and 5 , developments of BTT probes, signal preprocessing and vibration monitoring are reviewed respectively. Section 6 discusses future directions. Finally, brief conclusions are presented in Section 7 .

Funding Texts: Nowadays, microgrid (MG) has emerged to be a viable technology in exploiting various renewable energy sources (e.g. photovoltaic (PV)). Traditionally, the operation optimization of MGs is supported by the main grid. Given the intermittent and volatile nature of renewable energy, multiple microgrids (MMG) interconnect together have been considered to be an effective way to improve the security, reliability of the MGs [1]. It is well acknowledged that the cooperation of MGs can effectively reduce the overall cost of the MMG [2]. Consequently, motivated by various market infrastructures, collaboration of MMG has drawn the attention of researchers recently. The coordinated energy trading of MMG has been discussed in the literature [3, 4, 5]. According to transaction structure, there are three different categories for the operation optimization strategy. The first is centralized structure where MGs are managed by distributed network. In this way, the objective of MGs is to minimize the operational cost [3]. For this centralized mode, all interactive data are processed by the central controller. With the number of MGs increasing, management inefficiency is constrained by this method. To improve the management efficiency, top-down hierarchical framework is adopted as the second strategy [4]. In this architecture, the high level is operater (such as aggregator) which decides the price based on the generation cost and the demand and maximize the profit. MGs located in lower level schedule the demand to minimize their cost. The flexibility market enabled residential or industrial electrical prosumers (consumers and producers) to actively participate in the energy system by offering to sell the flexibility in their energy production and/or consumption processes. Distribution system operators (DSOs) offered to buy the available flexibility from the market in order to solve potential issues that might be caused by excessive distributed renewable energy generation, thus increasing the grid capacity margin without the need for expensive capital investments.

Funding Texts: Funding text 1: On the other hand, the prediction of the electrical power output is of great importance. In recent years, literature works are reporting that machine learning algorithms have become very popular and giving successful results in the prediction of PV power outputs (Elminir et al., 2007). For example, Said et al. studied the high CPV and the prediction of maximum power output with the artificial neural network (ANN) algorithm. In the related study, the authors calculated the R2 and MBE to be 0.988 and 0.009, respectively. Also, the authors highlighted that the power output data can be successfully predicted even with the small amount of data with ANN (Said et al., 2020). In another study, Anaty et al. investigated the predictability of power output in a CPV system with only a Radial Basis Function Neural Network. The authors compared the results in terms of only RMSE. In the results, the model developed in the related study was able to accurately predict the power output data of a CPV system (Anaty et al., 2018). In addition to ANN, there are also a number of studies using support vector machine (SVM) methods to predict the power output in PV systems (Zeng and Qiao, 2013). Considering the ANN and SVM together, in general, it is seen from the previous studies that the performance of these two machine learning algorithms has presented very close results to each other. However, the small number of input data is needed in the training of the SVM and is better in the solutions of nonlinear problems because the optimization step in SVM is automatic whilst the ANN structure is partially complicated in comparison with SVM (Wang et al., 2018). In another study, Wang and Koprinska studied on prediction of solar power prediction using kernel-nearest neighbor (k-NN) algorithm. The results achieved in k-NN algorithm was compared with those of NN, SVR (support vector regression), exponential smoothing and ARIMA. In the relevant study, the authors used only two metrics to evaulate the performance of the algorithms. These metrics are MAE and RMSE. In the results, the authors found that k-NN had the most accurate prediction results (Wang and Koprinska, 2017). In another study, power was predicted using ANN, SVM and KF (kalman filter) techniques by Monteiro et al. (2017). The results of the algorithms were compared with r, RMSE and MAPE. In the results, the best prediction results was observed by using ANN algorithm (Monteiro et al., 2017). Additionally, some researchers improved hybrid models to enhance the accuracy of power prediction results. For example, Eseye et al., studied the combination of wavelet transform (WT), particle swarm optimization (PSO), and SVM by using weather climatic variables as data inputs. In the results, the authors stated that hybrid models have better accuracy results in comparison with those of using algorithm-alone (Eseye et al., 2018). Similarly, Liu et al., studied modifying neural networks to reach the PV power results with higher-accuracy (Liu et al., 2018). In another study, Buwei et al., predicted solar power using ANN and SVM algorithms. The authors used original solar radiation, temperature, and relative humidity data to train the algorithms. In the results, SVM exhibited better performance than ANN for the prediction of solar power (Buwei et al., 2018). Sivaneasan et al., used ANN coupled with a fuzzy pre-processing technique to predict the solar power. The authors trained the algorithms with temperature wind speed, gust wind, solar radiation, and dew point data. In the relevant study, MAPE was calculated to be 29.6% for the best prediction result (Sivaneasan et al., 2017). In another study, Amarasinghe and Abeygunawardane compared the different machine learning algorithms (SVM, DL, and random forest (RF)). The authors predicted solar power output and the prediction success of these algorithms was discussed in terms of RMSE, MAE, and Bias. In the results. All machine learning algorithms had very satisfying results. For example, RMSE varied from 0.033 to 0.137, and MAE varied from 0.009 to 0.0138 in the relevant study. Considering all metrics together, SVM came to fore as compared to other machine learning algorithms (Amarasinghe and Abeygunawardane, 2018). In another study, Chu et al., optimized ANN with genetic algorithm (GA), k-NN and ARMA to achieve more accurate power prediction results. In the study, the authors used the cloud position, solar output power, clear sky index solar irradiance as input parameters. In the relevant study, MBE, MAE, and RMSE were discussed to evaluate the performance success of the algorithms. The lowest MBE, MAE, and RMSE were calculated to be 0.1 kW, 20.7 kW, and 35.4 kW, respectively (Chu et al., 2015). Ramsaemi and Oree predicted PV power output using GRNN, FFNN, and MLR algorithms, and the authors also proposed a new hybrid model as an alternative to these algorithms. In the results, the authors observed that the hybrid model had the best prediction results with RMSE, MAE, MBE, and of 2.74, 2.09, 0.01, and 0.932 respectively (Ramsami and Oree, 2015). In another study conducted by Marquez and Coimbra, GA was used to select the input parameters. The authors used ANN to predict the solar output. In the results, MBE, RMSE, and r were calculated to be −0.6, 17.7 and 0.947, respectively (Marquez and Coimbra, 2011). In another study, Pedro and Coimbra used five different techniques, namely the Persistent model, ARIMA, k-NN, ANN and ANN-GA for the prediction of solar power output. Based on the metrics, ANN-based predicting models showed better performance than that of other all models. RMSE and r values of this model is 11.42 and 0.97 respectively (Pedro and Coimbra, 2012). Gensler et al. compared the DL and ANN in terms of prediction to solar power output. In the relevant study, the authors reported that ANN was more superior to DL in the prediction of the power output of the PV system (Gensler et al., 2016). On the other hand, Wang et al. compared the different machine learning algorithms (SVM and k-NN). In the results, the authors highlighted that SVM was better than k-NN for the prediction of PV power output (Wang et al., 2018). Based on the previous prediction studies on solar power output, it can be said that the different algorithms are generally used to the power output of PV systems. Depending on the input data and models developed by the authors, the performance success of the prediction algorithms may vary. However, in general, the authors reported that all models are giving very similar results in terms of evaluation metrics. Therefore, it can be deduced that if the number of metrics is higher, a better comparison will be possible to evaluate the prediction models. In line with this, the present investigation deals with four different machine learning algorithms, namely (Support Vector Machine (SVM), artificial neural network (ANN), Kernel and Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) and deep learning (DL). On the other hand, R2, RMSE, MBE, t-stat, and MABE were used as evaluation benchmarks in order to make a better comparison among the machine learning algorithms.Machine learning (ML) is a very popular application type of artificial intelligence (AI) that generates a mathematical model depending on sample data, that is, training data. ML ensures the systems the ability to learn by itself and then to predict the unknown labels. A better regression prediction is strongly dependent on both the selection of relevant attributes and the accurate training of the algorithm. In this investigation, as mentioned before, it is aimed to predict the power output of a PV module. Firstly, the four different attributes regarding the PV power output were collected in this study. They are concentrated solar radiation, non-concentrated solar radiation, experiment time, and PV module temperature. Secondly, these datasets were used to train the four different ML methods. These are Support Vector Machine (SVM), artificial neural network (ANN), Kernel and Nearest Neighbor (k-NN), and deep learning (DL). The data linearly divided into two parts. The first part included the 3/4 of all data and they were used as training data. Then the remaining 1/4 was used as test data. In all methods, the same datasets were used both for the training and testing data, and the same labels were predicted in order to provide a better comparison among the ML models. All the methods were performed by using RapidMiner Studio Version 9.5. The characteristics of the top contributors might indicate vital information on the trend of publishing scientific studies. For example, Chinese authors and funding agencies were found to be the top contributors to the general computer science subject area. A benchmark study using studies published by Chinese researchers could be beneficial to the JICT editorial team so that the specific attributes of their studies can be identified and appropriate strategies can be taken to explore authors from China. Currently, JICT has received massive article submission of authors from India. Funding Texts: The paper studied a DNN approach for predicting the generators setpoint in optimal power flows. The AC-OPF problem is a non-convex non-linear optimization problem that is subject to a set of constraints dictated by the physics of power networks and engineering practices. The proposed OPF-DNN model exploits the problem constraints using a Lagrangian dual method as well as a related hot-start state. The resulting model was tested on several power network test cases of varying sizes in terms of prediction accuracy, operational feasibility, and solution quality. The computational results show that the proposed OPF-DNN model can find solutions that are up to several order of magnitude more precise and faster than existing approximation methods (e.g., the commonly adopted linear DC model). These results may open a new avenue in approximating the AC-OPF problem, a key building block in many power system applications, including expansion planning and security assessment studies which typically requires a huge number of multi-year simulations based on the linear DC model. Current work aims at improving the (currently naive) implementation to test the approach on very large networks whose entire data sets are significantly larger than the GPU memory. Copyright © 2018 IFAC 209 10.1016/j.ifacol.2018.11.703 Copyright © 2018 IFAC 209 In this paper, we report the new voltage control method with reactive power control using reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning is the theoretical framework to optimize an action of agent through trial and error in unknown environment. By using reinforcement learning, we do not need the detailed design of new system, and we can control the system voltage by re-use of the agent that has been designed before. Moreover, each agent can be controlled the system voltage on-line using proposed method even if an accident occurs. The purpose of proposed method is to bring out the cooperative reactive power control without the information between agents. We utilize the TD(0) method as learning method. However, we can obtain a pair of discretized state input and discretized action output in TD(0) method. We utilize actor-critic method (see J. Skach et al. (2018)) as a continuous value method of action output and approximation method with radial basis function (see R. S. Sutton et al. (1998)) as a continuous value method of state input. We verify the e↵ectiveness of proposed method through computational simulation using distribution network model.
